items.stem: What is the name for "the distribution of a solute between two phases, the basis of separation in gas–liquid chromatography"?
items.answer: Partition
items.markingKey: Partition: the distribution of a solute between two phases, the basis of separation in gas–liquid chromatography.

items.stem: In TLC on silica, a more polar compound usually has
options: the same Rf value as a non-polar compound
items.answer: a smaller Rf value
items.markingKey: It is adsorbed more strongly on polar silica.

items.stem: In GLC, why does a compound with a higher boiling point usually have a longer retention time?
options: It is more polar than the carrier gas
It is adsorbed onto the column walls
It moves faster with the carrier gas
It spends more time dissolved in the liquid stationary phase
items.answer: It spends more time dissolved in the liquid stationary phase
items.markingKey: Less volatile; partition favours the liquid.

items.stem: In a thin-layer chromatogram of food dyes on a silica plate with an aqueous ethanol solvent, the solvent front moved 7 cm and a spot moved 3.5 cm from the baseline. What is the Rf value of the spot?

An unknown mixture was analysed by thin-layer chromatography of food dyes on a silica plate with an aqueous ethanol solvent. The solvent front moved 8.5 cm. A spot moved 4.2 cm. Reference Rf values in this system: dye E 0.15, dye B 0.31, dye D 0.5, dye A 0.66, dye C 0.84. Calculate the Rf value of the spot and identify the component.
items.answer: Rf = 0.49: dye D

items.stem: Grace in a school laboratory tests a sample suspected to contain lysine and valine using TLC (amino acids on a silica plate with a butan-1-ol/ethanoic acid/water solvent). The solvent front moved 8 cm; spots moved 1.1 cm and 4.8 cm. (a) Calculate the Rf values of the two spots. (b) Explain why gas–liquid chromatography would not be suitable for analysing these compounds directly.
items.answer: (a) 0.14 and 0.6 (b) They have low volatility (strong intermolecular forces / ionic zwitterions or many polar groups) and may decompose before they vaporise; GLC needs volatile, thermally stable samples.
items.markingKey: (a) each [1] [2] (b) They have low volatility (strong intermolecular forces / ionic zwitterions or many polar groups) and may decompose before they vaporise [1]; GLC needs volatile, thermally stable samples [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the mobile phase in gas–liquid chromatography?
options: An inert carrier gas such as nitrogen or helium
items.answer: An inert carrier gas such as nitrogen or helium
items.markingKey: The gas carries the vaporised sample.

items.stem: What is the name for "a reagent, such as ninhydrin for amino acids, or UV light, used to make colourless spots visible"?
items.answer: Locating agent
items.markingKey: Locating agent: a reagent, such as ninhydrin for amino acids, or UV light, used to make colourless spots visible.

items.stem: Explain how separation occurs in thin-layer chromatography.
items.answer: Components are partitioned between the polar stationary phase (adsorbed on silica) and the moving solvent; components more strongly adsorbed move more slowly, so they travel different distances.
items.markingKey: adsorption to stationary phase [1]; solubility in mobile phase [1]; different distances [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how separation occurs in gas–liquid chromatography.
items.answer: The vaporised sample is carried by an inert gas through a column containing a non-volatile liquid on a solid support; components partition between gas and liquid; those more soluble in the liquid or less volatile take longer to emerge.
items.markingKey: partition between gas and liquid [1]; solubility/volatility [1]; different retention times [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a locating agent may be needed in TLC.
items.answer: Many compounds (e.g. amino acids) are colourless; spraying with a reagent such as ninhydrin or viewing under UV makes the spots visible.
items.markingKey: Many compounds (e.g. amino acids) are colourless [1]; spraying with a reagent such as ninhydrin or viewing under UV makes the spots visible [1] [2]

items.answer: Rf = 0.15: dye E; Rf = 0.84: dye C

items.stem: Kenji in a school laboratory tests a sample suspected to contain aspartic acid and tyrosine using TLC (amino acids on a silica plate with a butan-1-ol/ethanoic acid/water solvent). The solvent front moved 8 cm; spots moved 1.9 cm and 3.6 cm. (a) Explain why the two components travel different distances. (b) Predict how the Rf values would change if a more polar solvent were used, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) They have different affinities: the more polar component is adsorbed more strongly onto the polar silica and moves more slowly; the other is more soluble in the solvent. (b) They would generally increase: the components would be more soluble in the polar mobile phase and compete better with adsorption on the silica.
items.markingKey: (a) They have different affinities: the more polar component is adsorbed more strongly onto the polar silica and moves more slowly [1]; the other is more soluble in the solvent [1] [2] (b) They would generally increase: the components would be more soluble in the polar mobile phase and compete better with adsorption on the silica [1]

items.stem: Compare thin-layer chromatography and gas–liquid chromatography, explaining how each separates components and how the results are interpreted.
items.answer: TLC: silica/alumina stationary phase, solvent mobile phase, separation by adsorption/solubility; Rf = spot ÷ front, compare with standards, locating agents; GLC: liquid on solid support stationary phase, inert carrier gas mobile, separation by partition (volatility, solubility in stationary phase); retention times for identification; peak areas for relative amounts; limitations.
items.markingKey: TLC phases and principle [2]; Rf use [1]; GLC phases and principle [2]; retention time and peak area [1]; limitation [1] [7]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "integration"?

The relative area under each ¹H NMR peak, proportional to the number of protons in that environment.
The splitting of an NMR peak into a multiplet caused by the magnetic fields of protons on neighbouring carbon atoms.
Shaking a sample with D₂O replaces O–H and N–H protons with deuterium, so their peaks disappear from the ¹H NMR spectrum.

items.stem: Isla has two unlabelled bottles containing propan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH) and propan-2-ol ((CH₃)₂CHOH) and runs a ¹³C NMR spectrum of each. (c) Explain whether the two compounds could be distinguished using only the number of peaks. (d) State the solvent used in NMR and explain why.
